subject: lionDance
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: Chinese lion dance costume mid-leap.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm brainstorming a striking visual style for a mid-leap Chinese lion dance costume, weighing options like papercut/nianhua print versus a cloisonné enamel look with bold flat color cells divided by gilded lines.

I'm settling on the cloisonné style and now mapping out the costume structure itself — the head with its mirror, horn, mouth and mane, the cloth body with tassels and tail, and both dancers' legs captured mid-leap off the ground.

For grounding the pose, I'll keep the rear dancer's trailing foot just touching the floor as a push-off point, with the front dancer lifted high on the rear dancer's shoulders, head thrown upward — a classic lion dance leap that satisfies the floor contact constraint while still feeling airborne.

Setting overall scale now: lion body around 2.2m long, head roughly 0.7m wide and 0.6m tall, total height near 2.6m, then starting the skeleton hierarchy from the root.

I'm placing coordinates with the model facing +Z, rear dancer bent at the waist with hips around z=-0.9, one leg planted with a bent knee and foot near the floor, the other leg kicked up behind for the lift pose, chaining through hips, spine segments, neck, head, tail, and leg limbs.

Now I'm shaping the lion body cloth as a draped covering hung from the head down over both dancers, running from the tail through the rump, mid-back, and up to the shoulders behind the head, with fringe along the bottom edge and a width that varies along its length.

Right, the tube runs toward +Z so 90 corresponds to −X per the docs, and I want the hem fringe placed at angles around ±115–120 degrees along the sweep, hanging downward. I'll build frames at those positions facing up with a 180-degree lean and flow along +Z, then pass them into cards for the fringe effect, going for a cloisonné style on the body.

For the body's enamel look, I'm thinking of a Voronoi-style cloisonné pattern with gold wire separating cells of turquoise, red, deep blue, and white enamel. Rather than just using plain patches, I want to write a custom cell function that gives each enamel patch a domed look by blending toward a lighter center color based on distance, plus some warm top-lighting for extra depth.

Now I'm turning to the lion dance head itself: a big rounded Southern-style head with bulging ping-pong-ball eyes, a mirrored horn on the forehead, huge hinged jaw/mouth, mustache and beard, fur fringe, ears, and a prominent nose, all built with gold-wired details like the eyes. I'm placing the head joint slightly above and in front of the body, oriented to tilt upward as if mid-leap, and working out the local direction vector for that orientation.

Writing head geometry code...

I should pose the jaw at the end so earlier-built parts like teeth don't get caught mid-deformation. For eyes, I'm placing bulging spheres near the head's front with a gold-rimmed cloisonné texture—white enamel, black pupil, gold wire ring—mapping the drawing onto the sphere's front half and adding a separate flat pupil decal facing outward.

For the eye ring and lid, I'm adding a gold torus around each eyeball plus a partial hemisphere dome above for the upper eyelid, giving it a lion-like heavy-lidded look. The brows will be tapered, bushy blade shapes swept upward and back, colored white with gold edges.

I'm now adding a spiral horn on the forehead using a curved sweep, topped with a round gold mirror disc that glows cyan, possibly textured with a yin-yang-like motif.

Next I'm working out facial details: a bulbous nose, curved white whiskers along the lip, a shaggy goatee beneath the jaw, and a big ruff of fur rendered as cloisonné-style flame petals with gold outlines. I'm also adding white teeth with a red tongue, and large round ears on the sides of the skull.

For the body, I'm planning enamel cell patterns with gold wire, a dorsal ridge of gold pom-pom tassels along the spine, and an upturned fluffy tail made of curving segments ending in a tuft, all flourishing upward as if leaping. I'm noting that the "front legs" are really the dancer's decorated trousers holding the head aloft.

I'm working out the front dancer's pose during the lift: hips positioned forward and high with knees bent and tucked under the body cloth, feet in furry clawed lion-paw boots kicking forward, roughly sketching the hip-knee-foot coordinates for a bent, kicking leg stance.

The rear dancer sits lower, bent forward at the waist beneath the cloth, pelvis around y 1.0, legs spread with one foot planted and the other kicked back, legs showing below the hem as shaggy lion trousers with shoes.

I'm checking leg segment lengths against the distance to the ankle target to see if the pose is achievable, adjusting hip and ankle coordinates to get a more bent, spring-loaded takeoff stance without exceeding reach constraints.

Now switching to the rear push-off leg: positioning it extended behind with the ankle farther back so the distance check comes in under the threshold, allowing a believable straight-leg push. I'm also working out shoe geometry — small boxes angled so the toe touches the ground while the heel lifts, oriented along a forward-down sole direction for the planted push-off foot.

I'm thinking I could instead compute a bounding box over the whole root group after building and shift the root's y-position by the box's minimum, as a safety correction to guarantee the lowest point touches the ground, though I'm wary it might interfere with skinning or export behavior.

Working out the kicking leg's hip-to-ankle geometry, I'm checking the bend distances and deciding knee orientation points downward and back so the shin folds up behind the thigh, with the foot angled so the toes point back-down as if mid-kick.

I realize the kicked leg at z −1.65 overlaps the tail region, so I need to raise the tail higher, from around y 1.5 up to y 2.1, to clear the leg. For the rear legs themselves, I'm thinking of shaping them like the lion dance's shaggy fur pants — tapered cylinders with fur-card details and painted stripes to match the costume.

Now I'm setting up the chain structure for the limbs, naming the joints (hip, knee, ankle) for each leg and sweeping fur-textured geometry along them, with the rear legs parented to the hips and front legs to the shoulder/spine joint. I'm also working out the body's spine path, defining a sequence of points running from the tail base through the rump and up toward the front of the body to establish the skeleton.

I'll simplify by putting a hips joint as the root, with a back chain running to the tail tip and a front chain running forward to the neck, then sweep the body cloth along the spine's base separately from the fluffy tail sweep.

Still defining joint chains...

I need to sort out the head's local coordinate convention since right/left is flipped from what I'd expect—so I'm defining a helper where side=+1 means left (world +X), converting that into the correct negated local x value for head.local calls.

Now I'm working through the skull geometry: placing the cranium and brow as a sphere centered around (0, 0.22, 0.10) in head-local space, scaled to roughly 0.36 wide, 0.30 deep, 0.30 tall, figuring out how that scale interacts with the part's mesh-local axes.

I decide to be safe and explicitly pass `quat: head.quat` along with `at` for positioning, rather than relying on frame orientation defaults overriding correctly.

Now I'm working through each head feature's local placement relative to the nape joint, defining dimensions and offsets for the cranium sphere first with its enamel color.

Next I'm placing the brow ridge as a bulging sphere above the eyes to capture that classic protruding lion-dance forehead, then shaping the upper snout as a frustum box tapering from the face toward the muzzle, with a gold-trimmed lip edge planned along the front.

Continuing the facial build, I'm positioning the upper jaw as a wide flat box beneath the muzzle, adding a small gold nose sphere with dark nostril dots, hinging the lower jaw forward to attach the beard, placing protruding white eye spheres on either side, and finishing with flat disc-cylinder ears mounted toward the sides of the head.

Writing ear and horn geometry...

For the brows, I'm sweeping white curved bezier tubes from near the eyes up and back over the head, tapering to a point, possibly with fur cards layered in. For the mane and cheek fur, I'm planning to scatter fur cards across the cranium surface but need to filter which hits to keep so fur only appears on the back, sides, and top rather than the face.

Instead I'm settling on using ring primitives to create a mane ruff around the face edge—placing two overlapping rings of angled fur blades at slightly different radii near the head's base, tilted backward so they flare outward like a lion's mane, textured with a fur-flame pattern.

For color, I'm planning multiple tufts dyed in traditional lion dance palette—red-to-gold flame, jade green fading to white, and a separate white beard texture—so the mane reads as cloisonné-style fur blades with gold outlines rather than a flat tint. For the beard, I'm hanging a ring of elongated white-tufted frames below the jaw, flowing downward, though I need to figure out how to anchor them since literal frames without a bone reference will just snap to the nearest joint.

Teeth come next: eight small white boxes along the upper jaw and six along the lower, plus oversized canines, with a red box tongue tucked in the lower jaw—simplest to place these with explicit loop positions rather than a path. Whiskers are two long curved white sweeps from the muzzle, thin and tapering with small gold bead tips, and I'm considering adding pom-pom spheres along the head crest and body ridge for extra lion-dance flair, plus gold trim decals along the brow arcs, lips, and eye details to tie the face together.

Now I'm planning decals for the face and body: gold-wire "ruyi cloud" swirl emblems on each cheek of the cranium sphere, oriented outward at the correct surface direction, and larger gold cloud/coin emblems on the body flanks positioned symmetrically on both sides.

I'm also figuring out gold sash bands circling the body using surface loops cut across the spine at different points along the body, making sure the loop orientation follows the tangent direction of the sweep rather than facing outward.

Still writing sweep and tassel logic...

Now I'm thinking about scattering gold coin studs on the body, plus fringe cards hanging from the hem using a couple of textures, and considering adding fur strip cards for texture detail along the body surface.

Back fur cards (90) should use varied colored textures—red, jade, white, gold—alongside the eye, mirror, cloud, coin, bagua, and fringe emblems, totaling around ten textures. Now I'm designing the cloisonné-style card texture, sketching a flame/leaf shape path for its viewBox.

Writing SVG path code...

aring toward the top, so when flipped to hang, the knot ends up at the top with strands flaring down—that confirms my drawing orientation.

Now setting up the color palette: defining enamel paint hex values for vermillion, deep red, jade, teal, cobalt, indigo, ivory, gold tones, ink, and saffron.

For the enamel function, I'm computing cell distances to determine wire gaps versus filled color regions, adding dome-like shading that brightens toward each cell's center and warms toward the top while cooling at the bottom, plus a darker meniscus pit near the wire edges and gold wire coloring with slight noise variation.

For body colors I'm leaning jewel-tone: jade, teal, cobalt, indigo with sparse ivory accents for contrast against a vermilion-and-gold head. I'm sketching out enamel palettes per part now, assigning vermilion/saffron/deep-pink tones to the head and ivory/saffron/gold to the muzzle.

For legs I'm matching front and rear pants to gold/saffron/vermilion to keep the look linked throughout. I'm also budgeting the texture count carefully (eye, bagua mirror, cloud emblem, coin emblem, four fur tones, tassel -- nine total) and planning out the imports I'll need before writing the actual construction code.

Starting the builder setup...

Still building the chain hierarchy...

I'm sanity-checking the head placement and overall proportions — nape point, forward tilt, and total body length versus a real lion — and the resulting height of about 3 meters seems a bit oversized but acceptable for a stylized model.

Now I'm setting up the jaw joint attached to the head, defining a local helper for positioning it relative to the head's frame, and thinking through whether to use an aim target or a direction vector so the jaw bone orientation stays robust.

I'm also sketching a small helper function to generate head parts consistently, inheriting the head's rotation by default while letting individual calls override the bone or orientation—keeping the types loose since strict typechecking probably isn't enforced here.

I'm using a sphere helper to build low-poly head parts with flat shading, positioning and scaling the cranium mesh using the part options.

Now I'm working out the forehead bulge position and eye socket placement, checking how the eye sockets sit relative to the bulge and cranium front.

Repositioning the muzzle box and eyes so the eyes sit protruding above the muzzle, with the nose placed on top of the muzzle. I'm sketching a gold torus for the eye ring, orienting it to face forward along the head's local axis.

Working out the ring, iris, and pupil radii so they sit flush against the eyeball sphere at the right forward offsets, then giving the eyeball an ivory-white base color and shaping the eyelid as a tilted dome over the upper eye.

For the brow, I'm sketching a swept bezier curve going back and up like a flame shape, built as an ivory tube along head-relative points with a flat start and pointed end, plus a secondary gold underline layer beneath it.

Now I'm placing the ears as dish shapes angled outward and upward, using a cylinder for the red-gold rim and a smaller offset cylinder for the teal inner disc, with a possible fur tuft ring around the edge.

For the mane, I'm building a ring of blade-like cards around a line running up the back of the head, tilting them backward about 55 degrees so they point outward and back, and restricting the angular range to roughly -110 to 110 degrees around the top to avoid colliding with the jaw and open mouth.

Setting card sizes small and texturing them with fur variants, then placing two rings at different radii and depths for the mane with mixed colors. For the beard, I'm positioning cards along the jaw underside using horizontal and forward offsets.

Thinking through orientation: cards leaning 180 degrees point downward, so the drawing's tip ends up hanging at the bottom even though the texture itself renders "upside down" relative to its root—this actually works correctly for hanging fur flames and tassels since the root attaches at the frame and the tip extends away toward the ground.

For posing, since positions are defined before the jaw rotates, attaching cards to the jaw bone means they'll naturally follow the hinge rotation when posed later, which is what I want.

Now I'm working out teeth geometry—cones need to point downward from the jaw, but since quaternion rotation takes priority over directional vectors in my helper function, I need to adjust the helper so it skips quaternion application whenever a direction or aim vector is explicitly passed in.

I'm positioning the upper and lower teeth rows along the jaw edges, sizing canines larger than the rest, and defining the lower jaw slab geometry with its hinge point, tapering width, and enamel coloring, plus a darkened interior box for the mouth cavity when the jaw opens.

Now I'm adding the mouth's inner structure: a dark red palate plate beneath the muzzle and a pink tongue ramp sitting atop the lower jaw, with the jaw hinge rotating open about 24 degrees forward. I'm also placing the nose ball with slight flattening and gold coloring, small dark nostril spheres, and starting to think through cheek details.

Now I'm positioning red pompoms near the ears on each cheek, then adding cloud-swirl decals to the cheeks, mirrored left and right, checking that they don't overlap with the ear geometry or the cranium's ellipsoid shape.

Now I'm shaping the body sweep, defining a radius function that tapers width and height from rear to front along the spine and hips, with a slight downward shift to let the body hang naturally.

For the cloth draping over the dancer, I'm checking that the bottom edge clears the hidden hips at the rear, then setting the cloth's enamel thickness and cross-section detail with more sides for a smoother rounded look.

Skinning stays simple, one body sweep bound to spine and hips. Now I'm thinking through how to add a scalloped skirt hem using fringe cards, plus a gold trim sweep running along angled paths at the bottom sides of the body skin.

For fringe placement, I'll sample points along the body curve at increasing t values and orient frames at each using an up vector, letting unweighted frames default to the nearest rigid joint.

However, I'm now worried the nearest-joint logic could accidentally latch onto leg joints instead of spine/hips, since the leg joints sit close to the hem in x-position — so to be safe I should explicitly assign the bone rather than rely on proximity.

I'll just split the fringe cards into two groups: rear ones bound to the hips bone and front ones bound to a spine joint, accepting the rig isn't perfectly dynamic but good enough for the static pose.

For the back pom-poms I'll sweep points along the body path and stick small spheres embedded slightly into the surface. For the gold sashes I'll wrap loops around the body surface, building each loop from a frame at a point and tangent along the body path.

Then I'll scatter coin-like gold discs across the body surface with minimum spacing and a normal filter, adding ring trim to the loops.

Actually, simpler path: skip the coin texture discs entirely and use gold medallion decals instead — large ring-shaped emblems with a ruyi cloud motif placed on each flank of the body at two positions, mirrored across the ±X sides. I'm working out how the body's parametric surface orientation maps to left/right placement so the decals land symmetrically.

Now I'm setting up the tail as a separate joint chain branching off the hips, curving backward and upward through several control points, with a tapering radius and jade-enameled segments topped by a fur plume made of crossed cards.

Adding the ring of fur cards...

Now scattering more fur cards along the tail length (around 30), then moving on to legs -- planting the right leg and kicking the left, so I need a helper to define the leg geometry.

Writing leg helper and chain setup...

Now I'm shaping the shoe itself as a box oriented from ankle to toe, placed at the midpoint, with a dark enamel body and a gold toe cap sphere. I'm considering adding small ivory claw spikes near the toe tip for a lion-boot effect, but leaning toward keeping it simple.

For the planted leg's boot, I'm computing the ankle and toe coordinates, checking the box orientation angle for the sole, and verifying the leg reach from hip to ankle stays within the limb length limits so the pose remains anatomically plausible.

For the lifted rear leg, I'm placing the hip, knee, and ankle so the thigh angles forward-down and the knee bend direction makes sense for a push-off stance, then positioning the toe behind and below the ankle while checking it doesn't clash with the tail or torso.

I'm catching a potential overlap: the cloth's rear edge and rounded body cap could intersect the kicked leg's ankle position, so I'm nudging the body's rear z-coordinate and cap radius inward and adjusting the ankle and toe coordinates to clear the collision.

Checking leg geometry — thigh-to-ankle distances come out close to the reach limit, so I'm adjusting the ankle position slightly to introduce a small bend rather than a fully straight leg, confirming it passes safely below the body's hem rather than grazing it. Now moving on to positioning the front legs.

For the bent right leg, with a shorter reach of about .46, I'm thinking the knee hint should point forward and up, giving a high-raised knee like a dynamic leap pose—hip back at (−.14,1.4,.3), knee lifted forward, ankle tucked near (−0.2, 1.0, 0.55).

So the front dancer's left leg extends forward and down while the right knee lifts high, forming a leap stride, with the rear figure mirroring: left leg kicked back, right leg pushing off. I'm checking that the head, carried above by the neck/cloth collar, stays visually supported even though the connecting arms are hidden, and confirming the front legs sit within the body width so the rig reads correctly.

For the front limbs I'll give it a golden lion paw with claws, building a general boot/paw function parameterized by the ankle and toe points. I want to add a few glowing accents too -- a cyan mirror, slightly glowing irises -- and a small gold bell hanging at the throat on a red ribbon, lathed with a simple bell profile and attached near the jaw/head bone for that classic lion-dance detail.

Thinking about placement more, I'll keep just one big bell at the throat plus two smaller ones hanging near the base of the ears rather than adding extras on the cheeks. Now I'm writing the fur flame texture generator as an SVG flame shape with a gradient fill from root to tip color, gold outlines, and vein details down the middle.

Next I'm designing a tassel texture — a knotted gold bead near the bottom with five fanned strands rendered as double-layered strokes (a thicker gold base underneath and a thinner vermilion line on top) to get that cloisonné-style look.

Then I'm sketching the eye motif: a gold outer ring, an amber-to-saffron gradient iris, an ink pupil, small white highlight dots, and a few thin gold wire-like lines radiating from pupil to rim, all cropped into a circular frame.

After that I'm working on the mirror bagua design — a gold ring banded with the eight trigram line-groups in ink, centered around a yin-yang symbol.

Still drawing cloud lobes...

Still designing the medallion coin...

I should add cloud decals on the body flanks too, placing them near front and rear plus the mid medallion, giving three decals per side. For the decal placement on tilted body surfaces, I'm checking that the flank normal and position parameters work correctly on the vertical sides.

Now I'm defining an enamel paint function that uses cell noise to create a faceted gold wire pattern with light and dark variants, pulling in helpers like rgb, mix, cells, noise, smoothstep, and paint from the SDK. Writing cell-based paint logic...

Still computing darkened color...

I'm also setting up a gold metallic paint that blends dark and light gold tones based on surface normal and noise, while noting many shapes just use flat string colors, and I'm sizing the paint texture sheet appropriately for the builder.

Starting the full implementation file, importing the builder utilities and glow kit...

Writing build function and geometry helpers...

Now I'm mapping out precise head geometry coordinates for the cranium and forehead, working out positions and scale values for each sphere-based part to form the skull shape.

Working out the muzzle construction using tapered frustum boxes between two points, adjusting the width and height dimensions at each end to get a natural taper along the tilted axis...

I'm thinking through the lion dance mask's facial details now—a gold trim along the curled upper lip, a flourish moustache with swirled whisker tips, and placing the nose as a flattened sphere that protrudes above the muzzle's top edge, near where the forehead and brow ridges meet the eye sockets.

Working out whether the forehead bulge and eye spheres overlap, I'm repositioning the forehead sphere further back and down so it doesn't bury the eyes, then nudging the eyes forward slightly and checking where the cranium's ellipsoid surface intersects those features at various sample points.

For the nose and ears, I'm placing the nose just beyond the muzzle front, and figuring out ear placement by calculating the cranium's width at that height to decide how far outward and forward the ear discs should sit.

Now I'm working out the ear's directional tilt (outward, upward, back) and sketching a path for the horn using control points that curve from the forehead upward and backward, keeping the length modest like a lion dance horn rather than something dramatically tall.

I'm defining the sweep with Catmull-Rom curves, tapering the radius toward the tip, and planning banded coloring, a gold base ball, a small ivory pom at the tip, and a fur tuft ring around the horn's base. I'm also positioning a mirror disc on the forehead's front surface, working out its placement using the forehead sphere's curvature equations.

I'm figuring out the mirror's orientation with a forward-facing direction vector, plus its rim cylinder and glass circle components with texture, then shifting to defining the jaw joint hinge and lower jaw box placement.

Now I'm shaping the jaw taper using a frustum box, adding a chin lip curve, placing a red tongue box bound to the jaw bone, and positioning lower canine cones at the front corners of the jaw, making sure the mouth gap aligns with the muzzle bottom and jaw top.

I'm adding a dark interior fill plane inside the mouth cavity so it reads correctly when the jaw opens, setting the open angle to 22 degrees, and starting to lay out beard card frames arced along the chin edge.

For the chin beard, I'm planning an ivory-white fur texture with jade tips and gold vein accents for a traditional elder look, building the card frames before applying the final pose so the bone-relative positions stay correct.

Now I'm setting up the full fur palette: red-to-saffron, gold-to-light-gold, teal-to-jade, plus the ivory-white. The mane ring randomly selects between these colorways, weighted toward red and gold. For whiskers, I'm sweeping curved strands outward and downward from the snout using catmull splines, tapering the radius and tinting them ivory with gold bead tips. Next I'm working out cloud-shaped cheek decals on the cranium.

Now I'm adding gold trim details to tie the style together -- sweeping thin gold bars along the upper lip and lower jaw using curved paths, giving the mouth area a defined, ornamental edge before moving on to think about how the body connects to the head.

I'm checking that the body's front cap fits inside the head's cranium without poking through visibly, since the cranium is wider than the body's radius at that point, so the overlap should stay hidden.

I think there's a gap below the chin between the body and head that needs filling, so I'm adding a neck sweep—a tapered collar in body color running from the chest up to the nape—to close it off. Then I'm planning a ruff collar ring around the neck base at the nape, which doubles as the mane detail.

For the front legs I want big yellow furry paw-feet with claws, so I'm sketching a boot function: an enamel box for the foot with ivory claw spikes per toe, positioned by lerping between the ankle joint and toe point to find the midpoint and orientation.

Still working out the box dimensions, offsetting the center slightly toward the heel so the shoe wraps naturally around the ankle, then adding three small cone claws jutting out at the toe tip.

I'm also planning fur cuff rings at the ankle and knee joints instead of scattering individual fur cards, and sketching the hip sphere shapes where the front legs meet the body before moving on to the leg paint colors.

For the back, I'm adding scattered pom-poms in alternating vermillion, ivory, and jade with gold accents, plus a flame-like scatter of fur cards along the spine using a minimum-distance filter so they only appear on the upper-facing surfaces, leaning and bending them to flow downward naturally.

Now I'm working out the body's radius profile by interpolating arrays of x/y scale values along the body's length, giving it a tapering silhouette, and sketching out the main body path control points.

Still thinking through the body's bone chain, attaching the hip joint to the spine, and positioning dorsal pom-poms and hem fringe trim along the body curve.

Setting up color constants, pom-pom colors, and glow effects for textured parts, then defining the eye and iris geometry with proper facing direction and texture mapping.

Writing eye positioning logic...

I'm posing the jaw open at the end and skipping tail curl since front legs are already handled by IK. For the ground alignment, I compute a precise bounding box after posing and shift the root down if its minimum y dips below a small threshold, making sure the planted boot sits exactly at y=0 rather than any other trailing element.

Now I'm setting up the full color palette for the cloisonné enamel style...

Writing enamel paint function...

Still writing shading logic...

Defining remaining paint sheets...

I'm checking texel density across the body parts to make sure the wire gap stays readable at roughly 1.6mm per texel.

Drawing the tassel SVG with curved gold and vermillion strands plus an attachment circle and base rect...

Now I'm sketching the IRIS svg: a gold outer ring and an inner iris circle using a radial gradient to give it depth.

For the eye icon I'm adding thin radial wire lines in gold, a black pupil, a thin gold ring around it, and white highlight circles to make it feel glossy.

Then I'm moving to the MIRROR svg, planning a gold outer circle with a cyan glass center plus a shine sweep, and a ring of trigram bars drawn in ink along the gold band between the two radii.

For each trigram I'm computing the three bars per position (solid vs. broken based on bit patterns) and rotating each group by 45 degrees around center, then adding a small yin-yang symbol in the middle with white and teal halves, dots, and a gold outline stroke.

I'm now sketching out other decorative elements like clouds and medals, then moving into the body structure — fringe cards and tassels scattered along the sides, and defining a function to build leg chains with hip, knee, and ankle joints parented appropriately.

The chain also uses `chain.tip`. For the leg sweep, I'll vary radius evenly across the swept points with faceted sides for a non-smooth look, then define the limb function taking root, target, lengths, and bends.

I'm checking parent-child joint relationships: RL/RR legs parent off the hips, FL/FR off spine4. The bone connecting hips to each leg joint spans the distance correctly even though hips sits higher than the leg root, since bones just connect joint to child joint regardless of height difference. Now I'm working out where the front leg hip joints attach relative to spine4's position.

Now I'm defining the mane geometry: setting up a central axis line for the mane, then building two rings of card elements around it with varied colors, size, lean, bend, and spin to create a layered furry mane effect, with an inner ring set further back for depth.

I'm also sketching the brow shapes as a set of mirrored bezier curve sweeps, defining control points for each side's eyebrow geometry.

Checking that brow placement clears the eyelid dome geometry, then adding ear details with a gold rim, enamel inner, and jade bead center, plus small red pompoms on the cheeks. Now I'm defining the bell shape as a lathed profile, working out the radius and height points to form a closed, non-intersecting loop.

I'm reconsidering where the bells should hang -- rejecting a chin placement near the beard and instead deciding to suspend two gold bells from the ears via cords, positioning them symmetrically and working out the lathe profile with the bell mouth facing down.

I should also skip the neck chain sweep for now to keep things simple, and move on to writing the final code, making sure the skull part is correctly returned for the decal step.

Now I'm figuring out the decal placement and direction near the surface, giving it a glow effect, and setting up the mirror disc with its trigram texture staying dark where inked. Then I'm moving on to building the front legs.

Adding teeth loop logic...

I'll aim for around 600 lines, keeping it thorough but not excessive. I'm defining the hpart helper to default to the head's quaternion unless a direction, aim, quat, or rotation is explicitly given, then move on to body-related loops and a final gold ridge detail before wrapping things up with glow effects.

Still placing decals and stuck parts... working out the medallion and cloud decal positions along the body's front-to-rear path, confirming the flank decal orientation and that decals properly inherit bone weights from the skin. I'm leaving tail posing for later and sketching the lathe options for the bell shape.
